210	// checkoutOf is where a task's code lives right now.
211	func checkoutOf(t *task.Task) string {
212		if t.WorktreePath != "" {
213			return t.WorktreePath
214		}
215		return t.RepoPath
216	}
217
218	// annotate pushes the task's state and next action into the runtime as
219	// display-only metadata, so a sidebar can show why a session is open without
220	// anyone having to ask dev.
221	//
222	// For herdr this lands as workspace metadata tokens. A token only renders if
223	// the sidebar row layout in ~/.config/herdr/config.toml names it, e.g.
224	//
225	//	[ui.sidebar.spaces]
226	//	rows = [["state_icon", "workspace", "$stage"], ["branch", "git_status"], ["$next"]]
227	//
228	// Setting a token with no matching layout entry succeeds and shows nothing,
229	// which is why dev never treats a failure here as an error.
230	func annotate(app *App, rt runtime.Runtime, t *task.Task) {
231		if t.RuntimeHandle == "" {
232			return
233		}
234		kv := map[string]string{
235			"stage": t.State.Label(),
236			"next":  t.Next,
237		}
238		if err := rt.Annotate(ctxOf(), t.RuntimeHandle, kv); err != nil {
239			app.warnf("could not annotate the runtime session: %v", err)
240		}
241	}
242
243	func reportProvision(app *App, res *wt.CreateResult) {
244		p := res.Provision
245		if n := len(p.Copied); n > 0 {
246			fmt.Fprintf(app.Err, "   copied    %d gitignored file(s): %s\n", n, strings.Join(p.Copied, ", "))
247		}
248		if n := len(p.Linked); n > 0 {
249			fmt.Fprintf(app.Err, "   linked    %s\n", strings.Join(p.Linked, ", "))
250		}
251		for _, e := range p.Failures {
252			fmt.Fprintf(app.Err, "   warning   %v\n", e)
253		}
254	}

10	// openCheckout makes a directory live, asking the backend to treat it as a git
11	// worktree when it knows how — that is what groups the checkout under its
12	// parent repo in a sidebar instead of listing it as an unrelated directory.
13	func openCheckout(ctx context.Context, rt runtime.Runtime, dir, label string) (string, error) {

16		}

252	The branch is never deleted: removing a checkout and abandoning a change

278				// Close a runtime session pointing at the checkout first, so the

387			Use:   "plan",

389			Long: `Report the project types detected in this repository and exactly what

394	A worktree that comes up broken is the commonest reason people abandon

396	that depends on which lockfiles exist, which tools are installed here, and
397	which files are genuinely gitignored. This computes all of it and changes
398	nothing.
399
400	With --write, seed a .dev.toml from what was detected, so the repository can
401	commit its own setup and every machine gets the same one.`,
402			Args: cobra.NoArgs,
403			RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
404				ctx := ctxOf()
405				repoPath, _, err := repoContext(app, repoRef)
406				if err != nil {
407					return err
408				}
409				set := wt.SettingsFor(app.Cfg, repoPath)
410				plan := wt.BuildPlan(ctx, set, repoPath)
411
412				if write {
413					return writeRepoTemplate(app, repoPath, plan, set)
414				}
415				renderPlan(app, plan, repoPath)
416				return nil
417			},
418		}
419		f := cmd.Flags()
420		f.StringVarP(&repoRef, "repo", "r", "", "repository (default: the current one)")
421		f.BoolVar(&write, "write", false, "seed a .dev.toml in the repository from what was detected")
422		return cmd
423	}
424
425	// renderPlan prints a provisioning plan as a table plus its warnings.
426	func renderPlan(app *App, plan wt.Plan, repoPath string) {
427		fmt.Fprintf(app.Out, "%s\n\n", config.Contract(repoPath))
428
429		if len(plan.Ecosystems) == 0 {
430			fmt.Fprintln(app.Out, "No project type detected — only gitignored files will be carried over.")
431		} else {
432			t := NewTable("PROJECT", "MANAGER", "FROM", "DEPENDENCIES", "TOOL")
433			for _, e := range plan.Ecosystems {
434				deps := "—"
435				if len(e.DepDirs) > 0 {
436					deps = strings.Join(e.DepDirs, ", ")
437				} else {
438					deps = "global cache"
439				}
440				tool := "installed"
441				if !e.ToolInstalled() {
442					tool = "MISSING: " + e.Tool
443				}
444				t.Add(e.Name, e.Manager, e.Marker, deps, tool)
445			}
446			t.Render(app.Out)
447		}
448
449		fmt.Fprintln(app.Out)
450		if len(plan.Steps) == 0 {
451			fmt.Fprintln(app.Out, "Nothing to provision.")
452		} else {
453			st := NewTable("", "ACTION", "WHAT", "WHY")
454			for _, s := range plan.Steps {
455				mark := "✓"
456				if s.Skipped {
457					mark = "·"
458				}
459				st.Add(mark, string(s.Kind), truncate(s.What, 34), s.Why)
460			}
461			st.Render(app.Out)
462		}
463
464		for _, w := range plan.Warnings {
465			fmt.Fprintf(app.Err, "\nwarning: %s\n", w)
466		}
467		if plan.Empty() {
468			fmt.Fprintln(app.Err, "\nNothing would run. If a new worktree comes up broken, add what it needs to "+
469				"worktree.post_create, or commit a .dev.toml with `dev wt plan --write`.")
470		}
471	}
472
473	// writeRepoTemplate seeds a .dev.toml from the detected plan.
474	//
475	// Committing it is what makes a project's worktree setup reproducible: the
476	// next machine, and the next person, get the same one without having to
477	// rediscover it.
478	func writeRepoTemplate(app *App, repoPath string, plan wt.Plan, set wt.Settings) error {
479		path := filepath.Join(repoPath, wt.OverrideFilename)
480		if _, err := os.Stat(path); err == nil {
481			return fmt.Errorf("%s already exists — edit it directly", config.Contract(path))
482		}
483
484		var b strings.Builder
485		b.WriteString("# dev worktree setup for this repository.\n")
486		b.WriteString("#\n")
487		b.WriteString("# Committed on purpose: a worktree is a clean checkout, so without this a\n")
488		b.WriteString("# new one comes up with no dependencies and none of the gitignored files the\n")
489		b.WriteString("# project needs. Seeded by `dev wt plan --write`; edit freely.\n\n")
490		b.WriteString("[worktree]\n")
491
492		b.WriteString("# Gitignored files to carry into a new worktree. Only files that are BOTH\n")
493		b.WriteString("# listed here AND gitignored are copied — a tracked file is already in the\n")
494		b.WriteString("# checkout on the correct branch.\n")
495		b.WriteString("include = [")
496		for i, inc := range set.Include {
497			if i > 0 {
498				b.WriteString(", ")
499			}
500			fmt.Fprintf(&b, "%q", inc)
501		}
502		b.WriteString("]\n\n")
503
504		if len(plan.Ecosystems) > 0 {
505			b.WriteString("# Detected in this repository:\n")
506			for _, e := range plan.Ecosystems {
507				fmt.Fprintf(&b, "#   %-8s %-8s (%s) → %s\n", e.Name, e.Manager, e.Marker, e.Install)
508			}
509			b.WriteString("#\n")
510			b.WriteString("# \"auto\" runs those install commands. Replace with an explicit list if this\n")
511			b.WriteString("# project needs something else:  post_create = [\"make bootstrap\"]\n")
512			b.WriteString("post_create = \"auto\"\n\n")
513
514			b.WriteString("# How each project type gets its dependencies:\n")
515			b.WriteString("#   reinstall  run the install command (correct, the default)\n")
516			b.WriteString("#   copy       duplicate the directory from the source checkout (fast)\n")
517			b.WriteString("#   link       share one directory between checkouts (fastest, risky)\n")
518			b.WriteString("#   skip       leave the worktree without dependencies\n")
519			b.WriteString("[worktree.strategies]\n")
520			for _, e := range plan.Ecosystems {
521				switch {
522				case len(e.DepDirs) == 0:
523					fmt.Fprintf(&b, "# %-8s = \"reinstall\"  # %s uses a global cache; nothing to copy\n",
524						e.Name, e.Manager)
525				case e.CopySafe:
526					fmt.Fprintf(&b, "%-10s = \"reinstall\"  # \"copy\" is sound here and much faster\n", e.Name)
527				default:
528					fmt.Fprintf(&b, "%-10s = \"reinstall\"  # copy/link unsupported: %s\n", e.Name, e.Hazard)
529				}
530			}
531		} else {
532			b.WriteString("# No project type detected. Add the commands a fresh checkout needs:\n")
533			b.WriteString("# post_create = [\"make bootstrap\"]\n")
534			b.WriteString("post_create = \"auto\"\n")
535		}
536
537		if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte(b.String()), 0o644); err != nil {
538			return err
539		}
540		fmt.Fprintf(app.Out, "wrote %s\n", config.Contract(path))
541		fmt.Fprintln(app.Out, "Commit it so every machine provisions worktrees the same way.")
542		return nil
543	}
544
```

14	func newResumeCmd(app *App) *cobra.Command {
15		var (
16			noProvision bool
17			fetch       bool
18			force       bool
19		)
20		cmd := &cobra.Command{
21			Use:   "resume <task>",
22			Short: "Pick a task back up, rebuilding whatever is missing",
23			Long: `Make a parked task hot again.
24
25	Warm tasks still have their worktree, so this just reopens a runtime session.
26	Cold tasks do not: the worktree is rebuilt from the branch, which is why going
27	cold is safe in the first place — the branch, not the directory, is the task's
28	identity.
29
30	If the task is owned by another machine, resuming here takes ownership. Two
31	machines writing the same branch is the one way to make this workflow produce
32	a conflict, so dev asks before doing it.`,
33			Args: cobra.ExactArgs(1),
34			RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
35				ctx := ctxOf()
36				t, err := app.Tasks.Resolve(args[0])
37				if err != nil {
38					return err
39				}
40
41				host := config.Hostname()
42				if !t.OwnedBy(host) && !force {
43					return fmt.Errorf("task %s is owned by %s.\n"+
44						"Make sure that machine has pushed its work, then re-run with --force to take ownership",
45						t.ID, t.Owner)
46				}
47
48				if fetch {
49					if _, err := gitx.Run(ctx, t.RepoPath, "fetch", "--prune", "origin"); err != nil {
50						app.warnf("fetch failed: %v", err)
51					}
52				}
53
54				rt := app.Runtime()
55				mode := t.EffectiveMode()
56				checkout := checkoutOf(t)
57
58				switch mode {
59				case task.ModeWorktree:
60					_, statErr := os.Stat(checkout)
61					// Rebuild the worktree when it is gone — the cold-to-hot path.
62					if t.WorktreePath == "" || statErr != nil {
63						base := t.Base
64						// Prefer the published branch: a cold task's work lives on
65						// the remote, and a stale local ref could drop it.
66						if remote := "origin/" + t.Branch; gitx.RefExists(ctx, t.RepoPath, remote) {
67							base = remote
68						}
69						m := &wt.Manager{Cfg: app.Cfg, Runtime: rt, Log: app.Err}
70						res, err := m.Create(ctx, wt.CreateRequest{
71							RepoPath: t.RepoPath, RepoName: t.Repo, Branch: t.Branch,
72							Base: base, Label: t.Title(), NoProvision: noProvision,
73						})
74						if err != nil {
75							var exists *wt.ErrExists
76							if asError(err, &exists) {
77								t.WorktreePath = exists.Path
78							} else {
79								return err
80							}
81						} else {
82							t.WorktreePath, t.RuntimeHandle = res.Path, res.RuntimeHandle
83							reportProvision(app, res)
84							fmt.Fprintf(app.Out, "   rebuilt    %s\n", config.Contract(res.Path))
85						}
86						checkout = t.WorktreePath
87					}
88
89				case task.ModeBranch:
90					checkout = t.RepoPath
91					st, err := gitx.StatusOf(ctx, checkout)
92					if err != nil {
93						return err
94					}
95					if st.Branch != t.Branch {
96						if st.Dirty() {
97							return fmt.Errorf("cannot switch the canonical checkout from %s to %s: %s",
98								st.Branch, t.Branch, st.Breakdown())
99						}
100						if _, err := gitx.Run(ctx, checkout, "switch", t.Branch); err != nil {
101							return err
102						}
103					}
104
105				case task.ModeDirect:
106					checkout = t.RepoPath

110					}
111					if st.Branch != t.Branch {

113							"switch back explicitly or start a worktree task", t.Title(), t.Branch, st.Branch)
114					}
115				}
116				if t.RuntimeHandle == "" {

118					if err != nil {

121					if rt.Name() != "none" {

123					}

125

127				t.Owner = host

131				annotate(app, rt, t)
132
133				fmt.Fprintf(app.Out, "%s %s  %s on %s (%s)\n",
134					task.Hot.Icon(), t.Title(), t.Repo, t.Branch, mode)
135				if t.Next != "" {

144						app.warnf("branch is %d behind upstream — `git pull --ff-only` before you start", st.Behind)

30		// Markers delimit the region dev manages, so re-running it updates that
31		// region and leaves anything the user added by hand untouched.
32		blockBegin = "# >>> dev gitignore >>>"
33		blockEnd   = "# <<< dev gitignore <<<"
34	)
35
36	// osSection returns the junk files the host platform scatters through a repo.
37	func osSection() string {
38		switch runtime.GOOS {
39		case "darwin":
40			return `# macOS
41	.DS_Store
42	.AppleDouble
43	.LSOverride
44	._*
45	.Spotlight-V100
46	.Trashes`
47		case "windows":
48			return `# Windows
49	Thumbs.db
50	Thumbs.db:encryptable
51	ehthumbs.db
52	Desktop.ini
53	$RECYCLE.BIN/`
54		default:
55			return `# Linux
56	*~
57	.fuse_hidden*
58	.directory
59	.Trash-*
60	.nfs*`
61		}
62	}
63
64	const editorsSection = `# Editors and IDEs
65	.idea/
66	*.iml
67	.vscode/*
68	!.vscode/settings.json
69	!.vscode/extensions.json
70	!.vscode/launch.json
71	*.swp
72	*.swo
73	.nvimlog
74	.null-ls_*`
75
76	// agentsSection covers the directories coding-agent harnesses create inside a
77	// repository. The worktree entries matter most: an agent's linked checkout
78	// left untracked makes every `git status` in the main checkout unreadable.
79	const agentsSection = `# Coding agent harnesses
80	.claude/worktrees/
81	.claude/settings.local.json
82	.aider*
83	.cursor/rules/_generated/
84	.specstory/history/`
85
86	const envSection = `# Local environment and secrets — never commit real values
87	.env
88	.env.*
89	!.env.example
90	!.env.template
91	*.local
92	.direnv/`
93
94	// Compose renders the managed block from the given sections and extras.
95	func Compose(sections []Section, extras Extras) string {
96		var b strings.Builder
97		b.WriteString(blockBegin + "\n")
98		b.WriteString("# Generated by `dev gitignore`. Edit outside this block, or re-run to update.\n")
99
100		for _, s := range sections {
101			fmt.Fprintf(&b, "\n# --- %s (%s) ---\n%s\n", s.Name, s.Source, s.Body)
102		}
103
104		var tail []string
105		if extras.OS {
106			tail = append(tail, osSection())
107		}
108		if extras.Editors {
109			tail = append(tail, editorsSection)
110		}
111		if extras.Agents {
112			tail = append(tail, agentsSection)
113		}
114		if extras.Env {
115			tail = append(tail, envSection)
116		}
117		for _, t := range tail {
118			b.WriteString("\n" + t + "\n")
119		}
120
121		b.WriteString(blockEnd + "\n")
122		return b.String()
123	}
124
125	// Merge splices a generated block into an existing .gitignore.
126	//
127	// Replacing only the delimited region is what makes this safe to re-run: a
128	// project accumulates hand-written rules over time, and regenerating must
129	// never be the thing that loses them.
130	func Merge(existing, block string) string {
131		start := strings.Index(existing, blockBegin)
132		end := strings.Index(existing, blockEnd)
133		if start >= 0 && end > start {
134			tailStart := end + len(blockEnd)
135			if tailStart < len(existing) && existing[tailStart] == '\n' {
136				tailStart++
137			}
138			return existing[:start] + block + existing[tailStart:]
139		}
140		if strings.TrimSpace(existing) == "" {
141			return block
142		}
143		if !strings.HasSuffix(existing, "\n") {
144			existing += "\n"
145		}
146		return existing + "\n" + block
147	}
148
149	// HasManagedBlock reports whether a file already carries dev's markers.
150	func HasManagedBlock(content string) bool {
151		return strings.Contains(content, blockBegin) && strings.Contains(content, blockEnd)
152	}
153
154	// Detect infers which language templates a repository needs from the files it
155	// contains, so `dev gitignore` can be run with no arguments.
156	func Detect(dir string) []string {
157		markers := map[string][]string{
158			"Python":       {"pyproject.toml", "requirements.txt", "setup.py", "uv.lock", "Pipfile"},
159			"Node":         {"package.json", "pnpm-lock.yaml", "yarn.lock", "bun.lockb"},
160			"Go":           {"go.mod"},
161			"Rust":         {"Cargo.toml"},
162			"Ruby":         {"Gemfile"},
163			"Java":         {"pom.xml"},
164			"Gradle":       {"build.gradle", "build.gradle.kts"},
165			"Elixir":       {"mix.exs"},
166			"Terraform":    {"main.tf", ".terraform.lock.hcl"},
167			"Dart":         {"pubspec.yaml"},
168			"Swift":        {"Package.swift"},
169			"Composer":     {"composer.json"},
170			"TeX":          {"main.tex"},
171			"VisualStudio": {"*.sln"},
172		}
173		var found []string
174		for name, files := range markers {
175			for _, f := range files {
176				if strings.ContainsRune(f, '*') {
177					if matches, _ := filepath.Glob(filepath.Join(dir, f)); len(matches) > 0 {
178						found = append(found, name)
179						break
180					}
181					continue
182				}
183				if _, err := os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, f)); err == nil {
184					found = append(found, name)
185					break
186				}
187			}
188		}
189		sort.Strings(found)
190		return found
191	}

15	func newGitignoreCmd(app *App) *cobra.Command {

17			stdout    bool

19			noOS      bool
20			noEditors bool
21			noAgents  bool
22			noEnv     bool
23			list      bool
24		)

26			Use:     "gitignore [language...]",
27			Aliases: []string{"ignore"},
28			Short:   "Write a .gitignore from GitHub's templates plus the entries every repo needs",
29			Long: `Compose a .gitignore for this repository.
30
31	Language sections come from GitHub's published templates, fetched once and
32	cached. On top of those, dev adds the entries no language template covers but
33	almost every repository wants: the host platform's junk files, editor state,
34	local env files, and the directories coding-agent harnesses create — a
35	harness's linked worktree left untracked makes every git status in the main
36	checkout unreadable.
37
38	With no language argument, the languages are inferred from the files present.
39
40	Everything dev writes goes inside a delimited block, so re-running updates that
41	block and leaves rules you added by hand alone.
42
43	  dev gitignore                 # detect from the repo's files
44	  dev gitignore python node     # explicit
45	  dev gitignore --stdout        # preview without writing
46	  dev gitignore --no-agents     # skip the harness section`,
47			Args: cobra.ArbitraryArgs,
48			RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
49				ctx := ctxOf()
50
51				if list {
52					fmt.Fprintln(app.Out, "Available without a network:")
53					for _, n := range ignore.BundledNames() {
54						fmt.Fprintf(app.Out, "  %s\n", n)
55					}
56					fmt.Fprintln(app.Out, "\nAny name from https://github.com/github/gitignore works online.")
57					return nil
58				}
59
60				// Operate on the repository root, not wherever the shell happens
61				// to be: a .gitignore in a subdirectory only covers that subtree.
62				cwd, err := os.Getwd()
63				if err != nil {
64					return err
65				}
66				target := cwd
67				if g, err := gitx.Discover(ctx, cwd); err == nil {
68					target = g.Root
69				} else if !stdout {
70					return fmt.Errorf("%s is not a git repository (use --stdout to preview anyway)",
71						config.Contract(cwd))
72				}
73
74				names := args
75				if len(names) == 0 {
76					names = ignore.Detect(target)
77					if len(names) == 0 {
78						app.warnf("no language detected in %s — writing only the common sections",
79							config.Contract(target))
80					} else {
81						fmt.Fprintf(app.Err, "detected: %s\n", strings.Join(names, ", "))
82					}
83				}
84

86				fetcher.Offline = offline
87

89				for _, n := range names {
90					s, err := fetcher.Get(ctx, n)
91					if err != nil {
92						// One unknown language must not lose the rest of the file.

96					sections = append(sections, s)

102				extras.Agents = !noAgents

296	```bash
297	dev repo list                  # every repo under the scan roots, with status
298	dev repo clone owner/name -c Web   # clone into the right place, via gh or glab
299	dev repo sync --all            # fetch + prune, and report what moved

309	```
310
311	`dev stats` draws a contribution-style heatmap from two sources: a sampler
312	watching live agent sessions (the only way to count time spent reading and
313	debugging), and git history (which backfills the past and survives losing the
314	database). WakaTime can be imported alongside for editor time.
315
316	```bash
317	dev stats backfill                          # seed all repos from git history
318	dev stats backfill --repo api               # seed only one repo
319	dev stats sample --interval 5m              # from cron, every five minutes
320	dev stats import-wakatime                   # optional
321	dev stats path                              # durable SQLite location
322	dev stats clear --repo api                  # guarded selective deletion
323	```
324
325	In the TUI, select a repo and press `H`. If it has no data, `b` backfills only
326	that repo and refreshes the panel; `r` merely rereads existing stats data.
327
328	Stats are **data**, not cache: session samples and WakaTime imports may not be
329	reconstructible. They live at `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dev/stats.db` and clearing them
330	requires a scope plus confirmation (`--repo`, `--source`, or `--all`).
331	Regenerable data lives separately:
332
333	```bash
334	dev cache list
335	dev cache path
336	dev cache clear remote
337	dev cache clear gitignore
338	dev cache clear all
339	```
340
341	Those remove only `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/dev/{remotes.json,gitignore/}` and never touch
342	`stats.db`.
343
344	## Bootstrapping an existing machine
345
346	There is nothing to migrate for ordinary use: `dev` discovers repositories
347	wherever `scan_roots` point and never requires a particular physical layout.
348	When you want a recursive audit or a curated navigation layer, bootstrap is the
349	explicit path:
350
351	```bash
352	dev bootstrap ~/code /mnt/work                    # recursive report, no changes
353	dev bootstrap ~/code --json                       # machine-readable inventory
354	dev bootstrap ~/code --index ~/Projects           # plan a flat symlink catalog
355	dev bootstrap ~/code --index ~/Projects --apply   # create only the ready links
356	dev bootstrap ~/old --move ~/Projects             # plan physical moves
357	```
358
359	The scanner classifies canonical checkouts, linked worktrees, bare repositories
360	and symlink aliases, deduplicating by Git common-directory identity rather than
361	path.
362
363	**A symlink index is the default recommendation.** It gives a flat,
364	metadata-aware navigation root while every physical repository stays exactly
365	where it was. Put the index first in `scan_roots` and that alias becomes the UI;
366	normal discovery follows direct repo symlinks and deduplicates index + physical
367	paths.
368
369	Physical move exists, but refuses dirty repos, linked worktrees anywhere in the
370	clone, live sessions, a current shell inside, aliases that would break,
371	occupied destinations and cross-filesystem renames. A plan with any blocked row
372	moves nothing. `--config-out` writes a fresh config for the resulting root
373	without silently rewriting the user's current one. See `dev help bootstrap`.
374
375	## Adopting work in flight
376
377	There is nothing to migrate. `dev` discovers repositories wherever your scan
378	roots point and **never moves, renames or deletes anything** you already have.
379	`dev config init` probes the conventional locations — `~/Documents/Program`,
380	`~/src`, `~/code`, a `GHQ_ROOT`, and so on — counts the repositories in each,
381	and writes only the ones that exist:
382
383	```
384	$ dev config init
385	wrote ~/.config/dev/config.toml
386
387	Detected:
388	ROOT                 REPOS  ROLE
389	~/Documents/Program  40     scan root, new projects land here
390	~/src                16     scan root
391	```
392
393	Repositories are discovered; *tasks* are not. `dev adopt` finds the work
394	already in flight — linked worktrees from any tool, live runtime sessions, and
395	local branches ahead of the default branch — and offers to record it. It skips
396	branches already merged, and the turn-scoped worktrees an agent harness cleans
397	up itself:
398
399	```bash
400	dev adopt            # report only
401	dev adopt --apply    # record as tasks; nothing on disk changes
402	```
403
404	A worktree you already have somewhere else keeps working exactly as it did —
405	`dev` records the path git reports rather than relocating it. Full detail in
406	`dev help adopting`.
407
408	## .gitignore
409
410	```bash
411	dev gitignore                 # detect the languages from the repo's files
412	dev gitignore python node     # or say so explicitly
413	dev gitignore --offline       # cached and bundled templates only
414	```
415
416	Language sections come from [GitHub's templates](https://github.com/github/gitignore),
417	fetched once and cached. On top of those it adds what no language template
418	covers: the host platform's junk files, editor state, local env files, and the
419	directories coding-agent harnesses create — an agent's linked worktree left
420	untracked makes every `git status` in the main checkout unreadable.
421
422	Everything it writes goes inside a delimited block, so re-running updates that
423	block and leaves rules you added by hand alone.
424
425	## Configuration
426
427	`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dev/config.toml`. Write a commented starter with
428	`dev config init`; see the effective settings with `dev config show`; open the
429	actual file in `$VISUAL` / `$EDITOR` with either form:
430
```

1	# Parallel agents
2
3	How to run several coding agents without them stepping on each other.
4
5	## The one rule
6
7	> **Worktree per change stream. Pane per agent.**
8
9	Not one worktree per agent. Isolation should follow the *git mutation
10	boundary*, not the identity of who is typing.
11
12	```
13	one independent change stream
14	        → one worktree
15	        → one workspace
16	        → N tabs / panes
17	        → N agents
18	```
19
20	## When agents can share a checkout
21
22	They can, and often should, when **file ownership is clear**:
23
24	| Parallel work | Same checkout? |
25	|---|---|
26	| One researching, one coding | yes |
27	| Frontend and backend | yes |
28	| Tests and implementation | usually |
29	| `src/foo/*` and `src/bar/*` | yes |
30	| Both editing `package.json` | risky |
31	| Both changing one API surface | risky |
32	| Both running a formatter or codegen | risky |
33	| Both doing large refactors | no |
34	| Either running `checkout` / `reset` / `rebase` | no |
35
36	The question is never "how many agents?" It is **"can these two mutate the same
37	state?"**
38
39	## When they need worktrees
40
41	- Mutually exclusive *approaches* to one problem, to be compared and one kept.
42	- Unknown file ranges.
43	- Any agent that will run git operations changing HEAD.
44
45	```bash
46	dev wt create exp/jwt      --base main
47	dev wt create exp/session  --base main
48	dev wt create exp/oauth    --base main
49	```
50
51	Then compare, keep one, remove the rest. These branches are execution
52	artifacts, not architecture — they are meant to disappear.
53
54	## Two layers, two owners
55
56	```
57	outer isolation   dev      change streams a human will return to
58	inner isolation   Claude   turn-scoped subagent worktrees, auto-cleaned
59	```
60
61	Do not nest one inside the other. A `dev` worktree containing a Claude worktree
62	raises questions with no good answers: which branch am I committing to, who
63	cleans up, does closing the session delete the branch.
64
65	Inside a `dev` worktree, just run the agent — no `--worktree` flag needed. The
66	directory is already the isolation.
67
68	## Bringing environment into a worktree
69
70	Every worktree is a clean checkout: no `node_modules`, no `.venv`, no `.env`.
71	`dev` provisions on create. If an agent reports a project that will not run in
72	a fresh worktree, that is usually the cause:
73
74	```bash
75	dev wt provision      # re-run it
76	```
77
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
1	# Worktrees
2
3	A worktree is a second working directory for the same repository: its own
4	files, its own checked-out branch, sharing one history and one remote.
5
6	## What they are actually for
7
8	**Preventing two writers from editing the same files at once.** Not feature
9	management — that is what branches are for.
10
11	So the question is never "how many agents am I running?" It is:
12
13	> Could these two writers touch the same file?
14
15	- Different files, one goal → one checkout is fine. Several agents, several
16	  panes, one branch.
17	- Different *approaches* to the same problem → one worktree each, so they can
18	  be compared and the loser discarded.
19	- Anything where the file ranges are unknown → worktrees.
20
21	## Who owns which worktree
22
23	| Kind | Owner | Where | Lifetime |
24	|---|---|---|---|
25	| Feature, fix, experiment, handoff | `dev` | `~/Worktrees/<repo>/<slug>` | until done or swept |
26	| Turn-scoped agent isolation | Claude Code | `.claude/worktrees/` | dies with the turn |
27
28	**Might you come back tomorrow → `dev`. Dies with this turn → Claude Code.**
29
30	Never put a long-lived worktree inside the repository. Every file watcher,
31	language server, indexer and `rg` run in the outer repo then sees a second copy
32	of the whole tree.
33
34	## Commands
35
36	```bash
37	dev wt create feat/auth --base main   # create at the configured path
38	dev wt list                           # every worktree of this repo
39	dev wt open feat/auth                 # open an existing one
40	dev wt rm feat/auth                   # remove the checkout; branch survives
41	dev wt provision                      # re-run setup on an existing checkout
42	```
43
44	## Always pass a base
45
46	```bash
47	dev wt create fix/orderbook --base main
48	```
49
50	Without `--base`, a new branch starts from the **current HEAD**. Create a
51	worktree while standing on `feature/A` and `fix/orderbook` quietly inherits
52	`feature/A`'s commits. This is the single most common way to end up with a
53	history nobody intended.
54
55	## A worktree starts empty of everything untracked
56
57	No `node_modules`, no `.venv`, no `.env`. `dev` fixes this on create:
58
59	- copies the gitignored files listed in `worktree.include`;
60	- symlinks anything in `worktree.link` (opt-in);
61	- runs `post_create`, detected from lockfiles when set to `"auto"`.
62
63	Only files that are **both listed and gitignored** are copied. A tracked file
64	is already in the checkout on the correct branch — copying the other branch's
65	version over it would be wrong.
66
67	## Removing one
68
69	```bash
70	dev wt rm feat/auth
71	```
72
73	Never deletes the branch. A dirty checkout needs an explicit `--force`, and
74	that refusal is the feature, not an obstacle.
75
76	If the directory was deleted behind git's back, `git worktree prune` clears the
77	stale entry — `dev wt rm` and `dev sweep` do this for you.
78
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
1	# Parking and resuming
2
3	How to stop working on something without losing the thread.
4
5	## Why this exists
6
7	When the terminal multiplexer's sidebar is the only record of what you are
8	working on, nothing can ever be closed — closing it loses the thread. So the
9	sidebar grows until it is no longer scannable, which defeats its purpose.
10
11	`dev` gives that record a home outside the runtime. Then closing a session is
12	just closing a session.
13
14	## Pick a checkout mode first
15
16	A task is intent, not necessarily a worktree:
17
18	```bash
19	dev repo open api                         # ad hoc; no task at all
20	dev start api --task "typo" --direct      # current branch, usually main
21	dev start api --task "small" --branch-only --base main
22	dev start api --task "parallel" --base main  # default worktree
23	```
24
25	Direct tasks can go HOT ↔ WARM and finish directly; they cannot go COLD because
26	the canonical checkout cannot be removed. A branch-only task can go cold by
27	pushing and switching the canonical checkout back to its base. A worktree task
28	uses the full lifecycle below.
29
30	## The states
31
32	| State | Git | Runtime | Meaning |
33	|---|---|---|---|
34	| 🔥 hot | worktree + branch | session open | working on it now |
35	| 🌤 warm | worktree + branch kept | session closed | back within days |
36	| ❄️ cold | committed and pushed, worktree removed | nothing | paused, reconstructible |
37	| ✅ done | merged | nothing | entry survives until swept |
38
39	Aim for **three to seven hot tasks per machine**. That is a cognitive limit,
40	not a technical one.
41
42	## Parking
43
44	```bash
45	dev park --next "reproduce the token refresh race, then add a regression test"
46	dev park --wip                  # checkpoint uncommitted work first
47	dev park --cold --push          # push, then remove the worktree
48	```
49
50	`--next` is the part that matters. Without it, resuming means re-deriving where
51	you were from a diff — which is most of the cost of a context switch.
52
53	## Resuming
54
55	```bash
56	dev resume "token refresh"
57	```
58
59	Warm tasks still have their worktree, so this just reopens a session. Cold
60	tasks do not: the worktree is rebuilt from `origin/<branch>`.
61
62	That is why going cold is safe. **The branch is the identity; the directory is
63	a cache.** Once that is true, the local filesystem stops being a graveyard of
64	half-finished checkouts.
65
66	## Moving between machines
67
68	The remote is the handoff boundary. Do not sync worktrees or runtime state —
69	sync branches.
70
71	```bash
72	# on the machine holding the work
73	dev park --cold --push
74
75	# on the machine picking it up
76	dev resume <task> --fetch
77	```
78
79	**One writer per branch at a time.** `dev` records an owner host and refuses to
80	resume someone else's task without `--force`. Two machines committing to one
81	branch is the reliable way to produce a conflict here; the ownership check
82	prevents it.
83
84	If two machines genuinely need the same feature at once, split the branch —
85	`feat/auth-ui`, `feat/auth-api` — and integrate afterwards. Parallel writers
86	get parallel branches.
87
88	## Sweeping
89
90	```bash
91	dev sweep            # report only
92	dev sweep --apply    # act, confirming each change
93	```
94
95	Reports drift (hot with no session, a worktree git no longer knows about),
96	staleness (warm and untouched, clean and pushed → could go cold), and live
97	sessions no task claims.
98
99	It never deletes uncommitted work and never acts without `--apply`. Cleanup
100	usually fails not from unwillingness but from the absence of a trustworthy
101	guarantee that the work is recoverable. Reporting first is that guarantee.
102
```
</details></tool-use>

1	// Package help serves the git-workflow quick-reference pages dev bundles.
2	//
3	// These exist because the hard part of this workflow is not running the
4	// commands, it is remembering which one applies. A page you can reach in one
5	// keystroke from the terminal you are already in beats a bookmark.
6	package help
7
8	import (
9		"embed"
10		"fmt"
11		"io/fs"
12		"sort"
13		"strings"
14	)
15
16	//go:embed all:topics
17	var topics embed.FS
18
19	// Topic is one reference page.
20	type Topic struct {
21		Name    string
22		Title   string
23		Summary string
24		Body    string
25	}
26
27	// List returns every topic, sorted by name.
28	func List() ([]Topic, error) {
29		entries, err := fs.ReadDir(topics, "topics")
30		if err != nil {
31			return nil, err
32		}
33		var out []Topic
34		for _, e := range entries {
35			if e.IsDir() || !strings.HasSuffix(e.Name(), ".md") {
36				continue
37			}
38			t, err := load(strings.TrimSuffix(e.Name(), ".md"))
39			if err != nil {
40				continue
41			}
42			out = append(out, t)
43		}
44		sort.Slice(out, func(i, j int) bool { return out[i].Name < out[j].Name })
45		return out, nil
46	}
47
48	// Get returns one topic by exact name, or by unique prefix.
49	func Get(name string) (Topic, error) {
50		if t, err := load(name); err == nil {
51			return t, nil
52		}
53		all, err := List()
54		if err != nil {
55			return Topic{}, err
56		}
57		var hits []Topic
58		for _, t := range all {
59			if strings.HasPrefix(t.Name, name) || strings.Contains(t.Name, name) {
60				hits = append(hits, t)
61			}
62		}
63		switch len(hits) {
64		case 1:
65			return hits[0], nil
66		case 0:
67			return Topic{}, fmt.Errorf("no help topic %q; run `dev help` to list them", name)
68		default:
69			names := make([]string, len(hits))
70			for i, t := range hits {
71				names[i] = t.Name
72			}
73			return Topic{}, fmt.Errorf("%q matches several topics: %s", name, strings.Join(names, ", "))
74		}
75	}
76
77	func load(name string) (Topic, error) {
78		b, err := topics.ReadFile("topics/" + name + ".md")
79		if err != nil {
80			return Topic{}, err
81		}
82		body := string(b)
83		t := Topic{Name: name, Body: body}
84		// The first heading is the title; the first paragraph after it is the
85		// summary shown in the index.
86		for _, line := range strings.Split(body, "\n") {
87			line = strings.TrimSpace(line)
88			switch {
89			case t.Title == "" && strings.HasPrefix(line, "# "):
90				t.Title = strings.TrimPrefix(line, "# ")
91			case t.Title != "" && t.Summary == "" && line != "" && !strings.HasPrefix(line, "#"):
92				// A page may open with a blockquote or a list; the marker is
93				// formatting, not part of the one-line summary.
94				t.Summary = strings.TrimLeft(line, ">-* ")
95				return t, nil
96			}
97		}
98		return t, nil
99	}
100

```text
1	# dev and herdr
2
3	Read this when working on a machine that runs herdr, or when a task's state
4	should be visible in the sidebar.
5
6	## The division
7
8	```
9	herdr    per-host runtime: what is running, where the panes are, which agent
10	         is working right now
11	dev      cross-host intent: which change streams exist, what state each is in,
12	         what to do next
13	git      durable truth: the commits
14	```
15
16	herdr is deliberately **not** synced between machines, and `dev` does not try
17	to. Each host runs its own herdr; `dev ls --json` is the aggregation point:
18
19	```bash
20	ssh jingle-235 dev ls --json
21	ssh jingle-247 dev ls --json
22	```
23
24	## What dev asks herdr to do
25
26	`dev` shells out to the herdr CLI, which emits JSON for everything it needs:
27
28	| dev operation | herdr command |
29	|---|---|
30	| list live sessions | `workspace list` + `pane list` (panes carry the cwd) |
31	| open a checkout | `workspace create --cwd <dir> --label <name>` |
32	| open a **worktree** | `worktree open --path <path> --label <name>` |
33	| close a session | `workspace close <id>` |
34	| show task state | `workspace report-metadata <id> --source dev --token …` |
35
36	`worktree open` rather than `workspace create` for a worktree is what gives the
37	checkout git provenance in herdr: it appears grouped under its parent repo's
38	space with its own branch and ahead/behind row, rather than as an unrelated
39	directory.
40
41	`dev` does **not** call `herdr worktree create` — see
42	`worktree-ownership.md` for why.
43
44	Note that `workspace close` only ends herdr's session state. It does not delete
45	the directory, the worktree or the branch. That separation is exactly the one
46	`dev park` relies on.
47
48	## Making task state visible in the sidebar
49
50	`dev` reports two metadata tokens on the workspace hosting a task:
51
52	- `$stage` — `HOT`, `WARM`, `COLD`, `DONE`
53	- `$next` — the task's next action
54
55	A token only renders if the sidebar row layout names it. Setting one with no
56	matching layout entry succeeds silently and shows nothing, so add this to
57	`~/.config/herdr/config.toml`:
58
59	```toml
60	[ui.sidebar.spaces]
61	rows = [
62	  ["state_icon", "workspace", "$stage"],
63	  ["branch", "git_status"],
64	  ["$next"],
65	]
66	```
67
68	Which turns a row into:
69
70	```
71	● atp-sipui · HOT
72	  fix/gx-security-recovery ↑2
73	  finish the refresh regression test
74	```
75
76	That is far more useful than leaving four agents running in the hope that
77	seeing their names jogs your memory.
78
79	Because the layout is pinned by hand, re-check it against `herdr --default-config`
80	after a herdr upgrade — upstream changes to the default rows will not reach a
81	customised layout.
82
83	## Sidebar hygiene
84
85	The sidebar is working memory, not storage. Aim for three to seven hot spaces
86	per machine; everything else lives in `dev ls`.
87
88	`dev sweep` reports live sessions with no task recorded, which is usually where
89	the excess is. For each one, either `dev start` in that directory to track it,
90	or just close it — now that closing is not the same as forgetting.
91
92	## Agents are processes, not bookmarks
93
94	An agent pane with useful context in it is tempting to leave running forever.
95	Don't: herdr surfaces a resumable `agent_session` id, and `dev` stores it on
96	the task, so the conversation can be resumed after the process is gone.
97
98	Structure the isolation this way:
99
100	```
101	one independent change stream
102	        → one worktree
103	        → one workspace
104	        → N tabs / panes
105	        → N agents
106	```
107
108	Not one worktree per agent.
109
110	## Without herdr
111
112	`dev` selects `herdr` → `tmux` → `none`, in that order, and `runtime.backend`
113	pins it explicitly. The `none` backend prints a `cd` directive for the shell
114	wrapper instead of opening a session — so every core operation still works with
115	nothing but git installed.
116
```
</details></tool-use>

1	# Worktree ownership
2
3	Read this before creating a worktree, or when a new checkout is missing its
4	dependencies or `.env`.
5
6	## The confusion this resolves
7
8	Three mechanisms create git worktrees, and they all look interchangeable:
9
10	- `claude --worktree <name>` / `isolation: worktree` / `/batch` — Claude Code's
11	  own, under `.claude/worktrees/`.
12	- `herdr worktree create --branch … --base …` — creates a checkout under
13	  `~/.herdr/worktrees/` and opens it as a herdr workspace.
14	- `git worktree add` by hand, or a tool like Worktrunk.
15
16	They are all standard git worktrees underneath, so nothing *breaks* if you mix
17	them. What breaks is the mental model: two lifecycle owners for one checkout,
18	and no single answer to "where do worktrees live on this machine?"
19
20	## The rule
21
22	| Kind of worktree | Owner | Where | Lifetime |
23	|---|---|---|---|
24	| Feature, fix, experiment, cross-machine handoff | **`dev`** | `paths.worktree_path` | until `dev done` / `dev sweep` |
25	| Turn-scoped subagent isolation | **Claude Code** | `.claude/worktrees/` | dies with the turn |
26	| Everything else | **`dev`** | as above | as above |
27
28	**Might a human come back to it tomorrow → `dev`. Does it die with this agent
29	turn → Claude Code native.**
30
31	Concretely:
32
33	- Two agents implementing *different approaches* to the same problem, so the
34	  best can be picked → Claude Code worktrees. They are disposable.
35	- Two agents working on *disjoint files of one feature* → no worktree at all.
36	  One checkout, one branch, separate panes. Worktrees isolate change streams;
37	  panes isolate agents.
38	- A feature you will still be working on next week → `dev start`.
39	- Picking up on a different machine → `dev park --cold --push` here,
40	  `dev resume` there. The branch is the identity; the directory is a cache.
41
42	## Why `dev` does not call `herdr worktree create`
43
44	`dev` runs `git worktree add` itself, then calls
45	`herdr worktree open --path <path> --label <task>`.
46
47	The path policy has to hold on machines without herdr — a laptop, a CI box, a
48	server you ssh into. Delegating placement to herdr would mean worktrees land
49	somewhere different depending on what happens to be installed. Creating the
50	checkout with git and asking herdr only to *open* it keeps one policy and still
51	gets the full sidebar treatment: the workspace is grouped under its parent repo
52	with its own branch and ahead/behind row.
53
54	## Never nest a worktree inside a repository
55
56	`.claude/worktrees/` is acceptable for turn-scoped work because Claude Code
57	cleans it up and the directory is gitignored. For anything longer-lived, a
58	checkout inside another checkout means every file watcher, language server,
59	indexer, backup tool and `rg` run in the outer repo sees a second copy of the
60	whole tree.
61
62	`dev` refuses to create one, and will tell you to point
63	`paths.worktree_path` somewhere outside the repo.
64
65	If you do use `.claude/worktrees/`, keep `.claude/worktrees/` in `.gitignore`
66	so the contents never show as untracked files in the main checkout.
67
68	## Where dev puts them
69
70	Default:
71
72	```
73	~/Worktrees/<repo>/<branch-slug>
74	```
75
76	Fully configurable, because the right answer depends on the machine — a
77	different volume, a different naming convention:
78
79	```toml
80	[paths]
81	worktree_root = "/mnt/fast/worktrees"
82	worktree_path = "{{worktree_root}}/{{repo|lower}}/{{branch|slug}}"
83	```
84
85	Variables: `worktree_root`, `repo`, `repo_path`, `branch`, `category`, `host`,
86	`date`. Filters: `|slug` (filesystem-safe: `feat/auth/x` → `feat-auth-x`),
87	`|lower`, `|base`.
88
89	The reason for a separate root rather than siblings of the repo: with one or
90	two worktrees, `repo/` and `repo.feat-auth/` side by side is perfectly clear.
91	With ten, the projects directory stops answering "what projects do I have?" —
92	the filesystem hierarchy starts doing git's job badly.
93
94	## Provisioning: making a worktree actually usable
95
96	A worktree is a **clean checkout**. It has no `node_modules`, no `.venv`, and
97	none of the gitignored files the project needs to run. Without provisioning,
98	every new worktree starts broken.
99
100	`dev wt create` (and `dev start`) builds an inspectable provisioning plan,
101	then applies it. See the plan before creating anything:
102
103	```bash
104	dev wt plan                 # detect project types and show every action
105	dev wt plan --write         # seed a committed .dev.toml from the result
106	dev wt provision --dry-run  # plan for an existing checkout
107	```
108
109	The settings live under `[worktree]` globally or in the repo's own `.dev.toml`:
110
111	```toml
112	[worktree]
113	# Gitignored files to carry over.
114	include = [".env", ".env.local"]
115
116	# Heavy directories to symlink instead of copy. Opt-in and empty by default —
117	# sharing node_modules across checkouts breaks native builds often enough that
118	# it must never happen by accident.
119	link = []
120
121	# "auto" detects from lockfiles, or give an explicit list.
122	post_create = "auto"
123
124	# How installed dependencies arrive. The safe default is reinstall.
125	strategy = "reinstall"      # reinstall | copy | link | skip
126
127	[worktree.strategies]
128	node = "copy"               # override one ecosystem
129	```
130
131	**Only files that are both listed *and* gitignored are copied.** A tracked file
132	is already in the new checkout on the correct branch; copying the source
133	branch's version over it would be wrong. The classic mistake is listing
134	`.vscode/settings.json` — it is committed, so it is already there.
135
136	`post_create = "auto"` detects one command per ecosystem:
137
138	| Marker | Command |
139	|---|---|
140	| `uv.lock` | `uv sync` |
141	| `poetry.lock` | `poetry install` |
142	| `pnpm-lock.yaml` | `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` |
143	| `package-lock.json` | `npm ci` |
144	| `yarn.lock` | `yarn install --immutable` |
145	| `go.mod` | `go mod download` |
146	| `Cargo.toml` | `cargo fetch` |
147	| `Gemfile.lock` | `bundle install` |
148
149	A detected command whose tool is not installed is skipped, not failed. A failed
150	command is reported but leaves the checkout in place — it is usable, and
151	throwing it away would cost the branch for nothing.
152
153
154	## Copy, reinstall, link, or skip?
155
156	This is a per-ecosystem correctness decision, not merely a speed preference:
157
158	| Strategy | Effect | Default use |
159	|---|---|---|
160	| `reinstall` | Run the lockfile-derived install command | Always sound; default |
161	| `copy` | Duplicate the dependency directory from the source checkout | Faster where path-independent |
162	| `link` | Share one directory between checkouts | Fastest; usually unsafe |
163	| `skip` | Leave dependencies absent | Container/CI-driven projects |
164
165	`dev` encodes the non-obvious facts:
166
167	- Python `.venv` **cannot be copied or linked**: `pyvenv.cfg`, activation
168	  scripts and entry points bake in the old absolute path. `uv sync` uses a
169	  shared cache and is normally cheap anyway.
170	- Node `node_modules` can be copied, including pnpm's symlinks (links are
171	  recreated, not dereferenced). Sharing one tree is refused because an install
172	  in either checkout silently changes the other.
173	- Go modules are already in a global content-addressed cache; there is no local
174	  directory worth copying.
175	- Cargo `target/` can be copied, but is often larger than rebuilding. Sharing
176	  it is refused because concurrent builds write the same lock/artifacts.
177
178	An unsound configured strategy is not obeyed blindly: `dev wt plan` says why
179	and narrows it back to `reinstall`. A typo likewise becomes a warning rather
180	than silently skipping dependencies.
181
182	`post_create` and strategy are separate axes. An explicit command list replaces
183	the *derived install commands* but does not disable a `copy` strategy. A project
184	can copy `node_modules` and then run `make bootstrap`.
185
186	Per-repo override, committed next to the code so it reaches every machine:
187
188	```toml
189	# <repo>/.dev.toml
190	[worktree]
191	include     = [".env", "config/local.json"]
192	post_create = ["make bootstrap"]
193
194	[worktree.strategies]
195	node = "copy"
196	```
197
198	Re-run provisioning on an existing checkout with `dev wt provision`.
199
200	## Cleanup
201
202	```bash
203	dev wt rm feat/auth      # removes the checkout; the branch survives
204	```
205
206	Removing a worktree and abandoning a change stream are different decisions.
207	`dev` never deletes a branch as a side effect, and refuses to remove a checkout
208	with uncommitted changes without an explicit `--force`.
209
210	If a directory was deleted behind git's back, `dev wt rm` and `dev sweep` prune
211	the stale administrative entry instead of failing.
212
```

1	# Parallel agents
2
3	How to run several coding agents without them stepping on each other.
4
5	## The one rule
6
7	> **Worktree per change stream. Pane per agent.**
8
9	Not one worktree per agent. Isolation should follow the *git mutation
10	boundary*, not the identity of who is typing.
11
12	```
13	one independent change stream
14	        → one worktree
15	        → one workspace
16	        → N tabs / panes
17	        → N agents
18	```
19
20	## When agents can share a checkout
21
22	They can, and often should, when **file ownership is clear**:
23
24	| Parallel work | Same checkout? |
25	|---|---|
26	| One researching, one coding | yes |
27	| Frontend and backend | yes |
28	| Tests and implementation | usually |
29	| `src/foo/*` and `src/bar/*` | yes |
30	| Both editing `package.json` | risky |
31	| Both changing one API surface | risky |
32	| Both running a formatter or codegen | risky |
33	| Both doing large refactors | no |
34	| Either running `checkout` / `reset` / `rebase` | no |
35
36	The question is never "how many agents?" It is **"can these two mutate the same
37	state?"**
38
39	## When they need worktrees
40
41	- Mutually exclusive *approaches* to one problem, to be compared and one kept.
42	- Unknown file ranges.
43	- Any agent that will run git operations changing HEAD.
44
45	```bash
46	dev wt create exp/jwt      --base main
47	dev wt create exp/session  --base main
48	dev wt create exp/oauth    --base main
49	```
50
51	Then compare, keep one, remove the rest. These branches are execution
52	artifacts, not architecture — they are meant to disappear.
53
54	## Two layers, two owners
55
56	```
57	outer isolation   dev      change streams a human will return to
58	inner isolation   Claude   turn-scoped subagent worktrees, auto-cleaned
59	```
60
61	Do not nest one inside the other. A `dev` worktree containing a Claude worktree
62	raises questions with no good answers: which branch am I committing to, who
63	cleans up, does closing the session delete the branch.
64
65	Inside a `dev` worktree, just run the agent — no `--worktree` flag needed. The
66	directory is already the isolation.
67
68	## Bringing environment into a worktree
69
70	Every worktree is a clean checkout: no `node_modules`, no `.venv`, no `.env`.
71	`dev` provisions on create. If an agent reports a project that will not run in
72	a fresh worktree, that is usually the cause:
73
74	```bash
75	dev wt provision      # re-run it
76	```
77
```
</details></tool-use>

1	// Package cli assembles dev's command tree. Commands stay thin: they parse
2	// flags, call into the domain packages, and render. All policy lives in

14		"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/task"
15	)
16
17	// App is the state shared by every command.
18	type App struct {
19		Cfg   config.Config
20		Tasks *task.Store
21
22		Out io.Writer
23		Err io.Writer
24
25		// configPath is the --config override; empty means the XDG default.
26		configPath string
27		// runtimeOverride is the --runtime flag; empty means use the config.
28		runtimeOverride string
29		// noRuntime disables all multiplexer interaction for one invocation.
30		noRuntime bool
31	}
32
33	// Load reads configuration and prepares the shared stores.
34	func (a *App) Load() error {
35		cfg, err := config.Load(a.configPath)
36		if err != nil {
37			return err
38		}
39		a.Cfg = cfg
40		a.Tasks = task.NewStore(cfg.TasksDir())
41		if a.Out == nil {
42			a.Out = os.Stdout
43		}
44		if a.Err == nil {
45			a.Err = os.Stderr
46		}
47		return nil
48	}
49
50	// Runtime resolves the multiplexer backend for this invocation, honouring
51	// --runtime and --no-runtime.
52	func (a *App) Runtime() runtime.Runtime {
53		if a.noRuntime {
54			return runtime.None{}
55		}
56		backend := a.Cfg.Runtime.Backend
57		if a.runtimeOverride != "" {
58			backend = a.runtimeOverride
59		}
60		rt := runtime.Select(backend)
61		if h, ok := rt.(*runtime.Herdr); ok {
62			return h.WithMetadataSource(a.Cfg.Runtime.MetadataSource)
63		}
64		return rt
65	}
66

68	func (a *App) printf(format string, args ...any) {
69		fmt.Fprintf(a.Out, format, args...)
70	}

73	func (a *App) warnf(format string, args ...any) {
74		fmt.Fprintf(a.Err, "dev: "+format+"\n", args...)
75	}

14	// Repo is a scratch repository under t.TempDir().

20	// New initialises a repository with one commit on branch "main".
21	func New(t *testing.T) *Repo {
22		t.Helper()
23		root := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "repo")
24		if err := os.MkdirAll(root, 0o755); err != nil {
25			t.Fatal(err)
26		}
27		r := &Repo{T: t, Root: root}
28		r.Git("init", "--initial-branch=main")
29		// Identity and signing are configured locally so the test never depends on
30		// (or is broken by) the developer's global git config.
31		r.Git("config", "user.email", "dev@example.test")
32		r.Git("config", "user.name", "dev test")
33		r.Git("config", "commit.gpgsign", "false")
34		r.Write("README.md", "# test repo\n")
35		r.Git("add", "README.md")
36		r.Git("commit", "-m", "chore: initial commit")
37		return r
38	}
39
40	// Git runs a git command in the repo root and fails the test on error.
41	func (r *Repo) Git(args ...string) string {
42		r.T.Helper()
43		return r.GitIn(r.Root, args...)
44	}
45
46	// GitIn runs a git command in an arbitrary directory (e.g. a linked worktree).
47	func (r *Repo) GitIn(dir string, args ...string) string {
48		r.T.Helper()
49		cmd := exec.Command("git", args...)
50		cmd.Dir = dir
51		cmd.Env = append(os.Environ(),
52			"GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null", // ignore the developer's ~/.gitconfig
53			"GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM=/dev/null",
54			"GIT_AUTHOR_DATE=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
55			"GIT_COMMITTER_DATE=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
56		)
57		out, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()
58		if err != nil {
59			r.T.Fatalf("git %s in %s: %v\n%s", strings.Join(args, " "), dir, err, out)
60		}
61		return strings.TrimSpace(string(out))
62	}
63

69			r.T.Fatal(err)

1	// Package gitx wraps the git porcelain commands dev depends on. Every helper
2	// shells out to git rather than linking a Go implementation: git is already a
3	// hard dependency, its porcelain formats are stable and documented, and this
4	// keeps dev's behaviour identical to what the user sees when they run the same
5	// command by hand.
6	package gitx
7
8	import (
9		"bytes"
10		"context"
11		"errors"
12		"fmt"
13		"os/exec"
14		"strings"
15	)
16
17	// ErrNotARepo is returned when a directory is not inside a git working tree.
18	var ErrNotARepo = errors.New("not a git repository")
19
20	// Error carries the failing command and git's own stderr, which is almost
21	// always more useful than the exit status alone.
22	type Error struct {
23		Args   []string
24		Dir    string
25		Stderr string
26		Err    error
27	}
28
29	func (e *Error) Error() string {
30		msg := strings.TrimSpace(e.Stderr)
31		if msg == "" {
32			msg = e.Err.Error()
33		}
34		return fmt.Sprintf("git %s: %s", strings.Join(e.Args, " "), msg)
35	}
36
37	func (e *Error) Unwrap() error { return e.Err }
38
39	// run executes git in dir and returns trimmed stdout.
40	func run(ctx context.Context, dir string, args ...string) (string, error) {
41		// -c core.quotepath=false keeps non-ASCII paths readable rather than
42		// octal-escaped, which matters for the Chinese-named files in these repos.
43		full := append([]string{"-c", "core.quotepath=false"}, args...)
44		cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", full...)
45		cmd.Dir = dir
46		var stdout, stderr bytes.Buffer
47		cmd.Stdout = &stdout
48		cmd.Stderr = &stderr
49		if err := cmd.Run(); err != nil {
50			gerr := &Error{Args: args, Dir: dir, Stderr: stderr.String(), Err: err}
51			if strings.Contains(gerr.Stderr, "not a git repository") {
52				return "", fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", dir, ErrNotARepo)
53			}
54			return "", gerr
55		}
56		return strings.TrimRight(stdout.String(), "\n"), nil
57	}
58
59	// Run executes an arbitrary git command in dir. Exported for the few callers
60	// (park's wip commit, done's merge) that need a one-off command.
61	func Run(ctx context.Context, dir string, args ...string) (string, error) {
62		return run(ctx, dir, args...)
63	}
64
65	// lines splits git output into non-empty lines.
66	func lines(s string) []string {
67		if s == "" {
68			return nil
69		}
70		out := strings.Split(s, "\n")
71		filtered := out[:0]
72		for _, l := range out {
73			if l != "" {
74				filtered = append(filtered, l)
75			}
76		}
77		return filtered
78	}
79
80	// nulLines splits NUL-delimited git output (-z forms).
81	func nulLines(s string) []string {
82		s = strings.TrimRight(s, "\x00")
83		if s == "" {
84			return nil
85		}
86		return strings.Split(s, "\x00")
87	}
88

```text
1	---
2	name: dev-cli
3	description: 'Manage repositories and work-in-progress with the dev CLI: bootstrap existing machines, organise repos without destructive moves, own worktree lifecycle and provisioning, track HOT/WARM/COLD tasks, navigate via TUI, and bridge gh/glab/herdr/tmux. Use when starting, parking or resuming work; scanning or organising repos; choosing a worktree mechanism; fixing worktree setup; or cleaning stale branches, checkouts and sessions.'
4	---
5
6	# dev-cli
7
8	The `dev` command is a thin glue layer over git, worktrees, forges and agent
9	runtimes. It exists to stop four different things collapsing into one:
10
11	```
12	git remote      durable code state, the source of truth
13	git worktree    a disposable local checkout
14	herdr / tmux    a per-host live runtime
15	dev             human intent: what am I working on, and what is next
16	```
17
18	Everything derivable from git or the runtime is derived live. `dev` persists
19	only what git cannot answer — a task's **state**, **owner** and **next
20	action** — in one TOML file per task under `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dev/tasks/`.
21
22	**The problem it solves:** when a terminal multiplexer's sidebar is the only
23	record of what you are working on, nothing can ever be closed. `dev` gives that
24	record a home outside the runtime, so closing a session stops meaning
25	abandoning a task.
26
27	## Check it is there first
28
29	`dev` is not installed everywhere. Before using it:
30
31	```bash
32	command -v dev || echo "not installed"
33	dev doctor          # what works on this machine, and what degrades
34	```
35
36	Only **git** is required. `herdr`, `tmux`, `gh` and `glab` each enable more and
37	degrade cleanly when absent — never make a step hard-depend on one.
38
39	## Worktree ownership — read this before creating any worktree
40
41	There are three mechanisms that create git worktrees, and picking the wrong one
42	is the most common source of confusion. The rule:
43
44	| Kind of worktree | Owner | Where | Lifetime |
45	|---|---|---|---|
46	| Feature, fix, experiment, cross-machine handoff — anything you might return to | **`dev`** | `paths.worktree_path`, default `~/Worktrees/<repo>/<branch-slug>` | until `dev done` or `dev sweep` |
47	| Turn-scoped subagent isolation (`isolation: worktree`, `/batch`, `EnterWorktree`) | **Claude Code** | `.claude/worktrees/` (keep gitignored) | dies with the turn |
48	| `herdr worktree create` | **not used** — `dev` runs `git worktree add` itself, then `herdr worktree open --path …` | — | — |
49
50	**Rule of thumb: might a human come back to it tomorrow → `dev`. Does it die
51	with this agent turn → Claude Code native.**
52
53	Why `dev` does not delegate to `herdr worktree create`: the path policy has to
54	hold on machines where herdr is not installed. `dev` creates the checkout with
55	plain git and asks herdr only to *open* it — which still makes it appear in the
56	sidebar grouped under its parent repo with its own branch and ahead/behind row.
57
58	Never nest a `dev` worktree inside a repository. A checkout inside another
59	checkout makes every indexer, file watcher and `rg` run see a second copy of
60	the tree. `dev` refuses to do it.
61
62	Full detail: `references/worktree-ownership.md`.
63
64	## The task lifecycle
65
66	| State | Git | Runtime | Meaning |
67	|---|---|---|---|
68	| 🔥 `hot` | worktree + branch | session open | working on it now |
69	| 🌤 `warm` | worktree + branch kept | session **closed** | back within days |
70	| ❄️ `cold` | committed and pushed; worktree removed | nothing | paused, reconstructible anywhere |
71	| ✅ `done` | merged | nothing | entry survives until swept |
72
73	```bash
74	dev repo open api                                  # ad hoc; no task/worktree
75	dev start api --task "typo" --direct                # track current/main directly
76	dev start api --task "small" --branch-only --base main
77	dev start api --task "token refresh" --base main   # isolated worktree → hot
78	dev park --next "add the regression test" --wip    # → warm, session closed
79	dev park --cold --push                             # → cold, worktree removed
80	dev resume "token refresh"                         # → hot, rebuilt if needed
81	dev done --ff                                      # → done, integrated
82	```
83
84	**Parking is the move that matters.** `dev park --next "…"` is what makes it
85	safe to close a session, and the `--next` text is what makes resuming cheap.
86	Always suggest a `--next` when parking.
87
88	Full detail: `references/task-lifecycle.md`.
89
90	## Pick the task's checkout mode
91
92	A task does not imply a worktree. Use the lightest explicit boundary:
93
94	- `dev repo open <repo>` / REPOS Enter — ad-hoc open, no task at all.
95	- `dev start … --direct` / REPOS `d` — track current branch (usually main),
96	  create no branch/worktree. HOT ↔ WARM only; `dev done` needs no merge mode.
97	- `dev start … --branch-only` — create and switch a branch in the canonical
98	  checkout. No concurrent branch there.
99	- `dev start …` / REPOS `s` — default isolated branch + worktree. Use once work
100	  may be interrupted, experimental, or parallel.
101
102	Do not create isolation before it has a job, but do not carry dirty main changes
103	into a parallel task implicitly either: a worktree starts from committed HEAD.
104	Checkpoint first when the new task depends on that work.
105
106	## Everyday commands
107
108	```bash
109	dev                        # interactive dashboard (plain listing when piped)
110	dev edit                   # open the effective config; generate it first if absent
111	dev ls                     # what am I working on, everywhere
112	dev ls --json              # stable machine-readable form (also over ssh)
113	dev status                 # what is this directory: repo, branch, task, session
114	dev sweep                  # what has gone stale or drifted, and what to do
115	dev sweep --apply          # act on it, confirming each change
116
117	dev wt create feat/auth --base main    # worktree at the configured path
118	dev wt list                            # every worktree of this repo
119	dev wt plan                            # what a new worktree would be set up with
120	dev wt plan --write                    # seed a committed .dev.toml from it
121	dev wt rm feat/auth                    # remove the checkout; the branch stays
122
123	dev repo list              # every repo under the scan roots
124	dev repo clone owner/name  # clone into the right place, via gh or glab
125	dev repo sync --all        # fetch + prune, and report what moved
126	dev repo remote [query]     # search authenticated gh + glab repositories
127	dev bootstrap ~/code       # recursively inventory an existing machine
128	dev bootstrap ~/code --index ~/Projects   # plan a non-destructive symlink catalog
129	dev gitignore              # .gitignore from GitHub templates + the common bits
130	dev adopt                  # import existing worktrees/sessions/branches as tasks
131
132	dev try redis-streams      # dated scratch directory for an experiment
133	dev graduate redis-streams --category Infra   # promote it into a real project
134
135	dev stats --heatmap        # where the time actually went
136	dev stats backfill --repo api  # seed one repo; TUI H then b does this in place
137	dev stats path             # durable XDG data, not cache
138	dev cache list             # regenerable forge/gitignore caches
139	dev help worktrees         # quick-reference pages
140	```
141
142	Complete generated reference: `references/commands.md`.
143
144	## Bootstrapping and adopting an existing machine
145
146	Read `references/bootstrap.md` before recursively scanning paths, creating a
147	symlink index, moving physical repositories, or generating layout config. Move
148	is destructive and must follow its report → review → apply procedure.
149
150	There is nothing to migrate for ordinary use. `dev` discovers repositories through
151	`paths.scan_roots` and never moves, renames or deletes anything.
152
153	```bash
154	dev config init     # detects this machine's roots; every value stays editable
155	dev adopt           # report existing worktrees, sessions and unmerged branches
156	dev adopt --apply   # record them as tasks (nothing on disk changes)
157	```
158
159	Do not assume the user's layout is `~/Documents/Program`. Run `dev config show`
160	or `dev repo list` to see what this machine is actually configured for.
161
162	## Dashboard and forge inventory
163
164	The TUI has TASKS, REPOS and REMOTE views, switched with tab or vim-style h/l.
165	REMOTE queries authenticated `gh` and `glab` lazily, uses a short-lived private
166	cache, and `/` filters provider, owner/name and description. Enter opens a local
167	clone; `c` confirms before cloning an absent remote. Use `dev repo remote
168	[query] --json` for the non-interactive form; `--cached` avoids a network query.
169
170	REPOS has explicit LIVE and LATEST columns: latest is the newest dirty-file
171	mtime, commit, or task update. Detail shows the Herdr/tmux handle and agent
172	status. `[tui.repos]` chooses columns and default sort; `O` cycles sort and `R`
173	reverses it.
174
175	`H` opens the selected repo's heatmap. On an empty panel, `b` backfills only
176	that repo and redraws; `r` rereads existing stats. Stats live in
177	`$XDG_DATA_HOME/dev/stats.db` and are durable observations, not cache — use
178	`dev stats clear` with an explicit scope. `dev cache clear` only removes
179	regenerable forge/gitignore data under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/dev`.
180
181	`e` edits config and returning live-reloads data/tool bindings; `r` reloads
182	explicitly. Runtime
183	backend changes require restarting the TUI.
184
185	External tools are explicit `[[tui.tools]]` config. Run `dev tui tools` before
186	recommending a binding; it shows the exact command and whether it is available.
187	Commands run through `$SHELL` in the selected checkout. For an alias/function
188	that exists only in shell rc, set `interactive = true`; dev uses `$SHELL -lic`
189	and evaluates the command after rc loading. Prefer an executable on PATH when
190	the binding should be portable across machines.
191
192	## Editing configuration
193
194	Use `dev edit` (or `dev config edit`) rather than guessing the XDG path. It
195	opens the file selected by `--config`, generating the machine-detected starter
196	when absent, and resolves `--editor` → `$VISUAL` → `$EDITOR` → nvim/vim/vi.
197
198	## Rules for agents
199
200	1. **Do not equate task with worktree.** Ad-hoc opening needs no task; `--direct`
201	   tracks current/main; `--branch-only` is lightweight isolation; default
202	   worktree is for interruption/experimentation/parallelism.
203
204	2. **Always pass `--base` for branch/worktree tasks.** Without it a new branch starts from the current
205	   HEAD, so starting a task while standing on `feature/A` silently builds on
206	   `feature/A`. This is the single most common way to produce a confusing
207	   history unattended.
208
209	3. **Never `--force` a worktree removal on your own.** `dev wt rm` refuses a
210	   checkout with uncommitted changes; that refusal is the feature. Ask the
211	   user before overriding it.
212
213	4. **Report drift, do not fix it silently.** `dev sweep` without `--apply`
214	   changes nothing. Show the user its output rather than running `--apply --yes`
215	   for them.
216
217	5. **Prefer a checkpoint commit over `git stash`.** A stash is invisible in the
218	   log, easy to forget, and cannot be pushed — so it can never reach another
219	   machine. `dev park --wip` makes a `wip:` commit instead.
220
221	6. **One writer per branch at a time.** `dev resume` refuses a task owned by
222	   another host without `--force`. Before overriding, confirm that machine has
223	   pushed.
224
225	7. **Check `dev wt plan` before blaming a worktree.** A worktree that comes up
226	   broken is nearly always a provisioning gap, not a git problem. The plan
227	   shows the detected project types, which tools are missing, and exactly what
228	   would be copied or run. Dependencies arrive by a per-ecosystem strategy —
229	   `reinstall` (default), `copy`, `link` or `skip` — and dev refuses an unsound
230	   one rather than producing a broken checkout: a virtualenv cannot be copied,
231	   because it bakes its own absolute path into `pyvenv.cfg`.
232
233	8. **Do not create a worktree per agent.** Worktrees isolate *change streams*;
234	   panes isolate *agents*. Several agents working on disjoint files of one
235	   feature belong in one checkout.
236
237	9. **Prefer `dev bootstrap --index` over `--move`.** If the problem is
238	   navigation, a symlink catalog solves it without changing the authoritative
239	   paths. For a physical move, never add `--apply --yes` on the user's behalf;
240	   blocked rows are preconditions to resolve, not checks to bypass.
241
242	10. **`dev adopt` without `--apply` changes nothing.** Show the user its report
243	   rather than applying it for them — which branches count as work in flight is
244	   their judgement, not yours.
245
246	11. **Do not call stats.db a cache.** Session/WakaTime observations may not be
247	   reconstructible. Use `dev stats clear --repo/--source/--all`; use
248	   `dev cache clear` only for remote/gitignore caches.
249
250	12. **Read Git state as counts, not a dirty boolean.** `⇡`/`⇣` are upstream
251	   divergence; `=` conflicts, `+` staged, `!` unstaged, `?` untracked. Use
252	   `dev status` or JSON for the unique-path and type breakdown before cleanup.
253
254	13. **Commit messages stay English** and follow Conventional Commits, even when
255	   the conversation is in another language — see the companion `git-workflow`
256	   skill, which owns commit conventions, SemVer and branch naming. This skill
257	   does not duplicate them.
258
259	## When to use this skill
260
261	- "What am I working on?" / "我在做什麼" / too many terminal workspaces open.
262	- Starting, parking or resuming a piece of work.
263	- "Where should this worktree go?" / "should I use `claude --worktree` or herdr?"
264	- A new worktree is missing `node_modules`, `.venv` or `.env`.
265	- Cleaning up stale branches, worktrees and sessions.
266	- Cloning, creating or auditing repositories across a machine.
267	- Promoting an experiment into a real project.
268	- "Which repo do I spend my time in?"
269	- Setting up a `.gitignore`, or a harness worktree showing as untracked.
270	- Adopting a machine that already has repos, worktrees and sessions.
271	- Recursively scanning, indexing, or physically reorganising existing repos.
272	- Configuring a flat repo/worktree layout or generating config for one.
273
274	## When NOT to use it
275
276	- **Commit messages, SemVer, branch naming, PR-vs-main tiering** — that is the
277	  `git-workflow` skill. This one links to it rather than restating it.
278	- **Driving herdr panes and agents directly** — that is the `herdr` skill.
279	- A single `git add` + `git commit` needs no tooling at all.
280
281	## Reference files
282
283	- `references/bootstrap.md` — read before scanning or organising an existing
284	  machine; includes the non-destructive index default and move safety gates.
285	- `references/worktree-ownership.md` — who owns which worktree, and how a
286	  worktree gets a working environment. Read before creating one.
287	- `references/task-lifecycle.md` — HOT/WARM/COLD/DONE, when to park, and how
288	  work moves between machines.
289	- `references/runtime-herdr.md` — how `dev` and herdr divide responsibility,
290	  and the sidebar configuration that makes task state visible.
291	- `references/commands.md` — the full command reference, generated from the
292	  binary by `dev skill sync` so it cannot drift.
293
294	## Gotchas
295
296	- **`dev` is a shell function, not just a binary.** Commands that move you into
297	  a checkout print a `cd` directive for the wrapper installed by
298	  `eval "$(dev shell-init zsh)"`. Without it they print a path and do not move
299	  you — that is not a bug.
300	- **A worktree is a clean checkout.** It has no `node_modules`, no `.venv` and
301	  none of the gitignored env files. `dev` provisions it; `--no-provision`
302	  skips that and leaves you to it.
303	- **Only gitignored files are copied into a worktree.** Listing a *tracked*
304	  file in `worktree.include` does nothing, because git already put it there on
305	  the correct branch — and copying it would overwrite that version.
306	- **Removing a worktree never deletes the branch.** Those are separate
307	  decisions; conflating them is how work gets lost.
308	- **`dev done` defaults to reporting.** With neither `--ff` nor `--pr` it
309	  explains the options and changes nothing.
310	- **The stats sampler must be scheduled.** `dev stats` is empty until
311	  `dev stats backfill` runs once and `dev stats sample` runs periodically.
312

```text
1	# dev and herdr
2
3	Read this when working on a machine that runs herdr, or when a task's state
4	should be visible in the sidebar.
5
6	## The division
7
8	```
9	herdr    per-host runtime: what is running, where the panes are, which agent
10	         is working right now
11	dev      cross-host intent: which change streams exist, what state each is in,
12	         what to do next
13	git      durable truth: the commits
14	```
15
16	herdr is deliberately **not** synced between machines, and `dev` does not try
17	to. Each host runs its own herdr; `dev ls --json` is the aggregation point:
18
19	```bash
20	ssh jingle-235 dev ls --json
21	ssh jingle-247 dev ls --json
22	```
23
24	## What dev asks herdr to do
25
26	`dev` shells out to the herdr CLI, which emits JSON for everything it needs:
27
28	| dev operation | herdr command |
29	|---|---|
30	| list live sessions | `workspace list` + `pane list` (panes carry the cwd) |
31	| open a checkout | `workspace create --cwd <dir> --label <name>` |
32	| open a **worktree** | `worktree open --path <path> --label <name>` |
33	| close a session | `workspace close <id>` |
34	| show task state | `workspace report-metadata <id> --source dev --token …` |
35
36	`worktree open` rather than `workspace create` for a worktree is what gives the
37	checkout git provenance in herdr: it appears grouped under its parent repo's
38	space with its own branch and ahead/behind row, rather than as an unrelated
39	directory.
40
41	`dev` does **not** call `herdr worktree create` — see
42	`worktree-ownership.md` for why.
43
44	Note that `workspace close` only ends herdr's session state. It does not delete
45	the directory, the worktree or the branch. That separation is exactly the one
46	`dev park` relies on.
47
48	## Making task state visible in the sidebar
49
50	`dev` reports two metadata tokens on the workspace hosting a task:
51
52	- `$stage` — `HOT`, `WARM`, `COLD`, `DONE`
53	- `$next` — the task's next action
54
55	A token only renders if the sidebar row layout names it. Setting one with no
56	matching layout entry succeeds silently and shows nothing, so add this to
57	`~/.config/herdr/config.toml`:
58
59	```toml
60	[ui.sidebar.spaces]
61	rows = [
62	  ["state_icon", "workspace", "$stage"],
63	  ["branch", "git_status"],
64	  ["$next"],
65	]
66	```
67
68	Which turns a row into:
69
70	```
71	● atp-sipui · HOT
72	  fix/gx-security-recovery ↑2
73	  finish the refresh regression test
74	```
75
76	That is far more useful than leaving four agents running in the hope that
77	seeing their names jogs your memory.
78
79	Because the layout is pinned by hand, re-check it against `herdr --default-config`
80	after a herdr upgrade — upstream changes to the default rows will not reach a
81	customised layout.
82
83	## Sidebar hygiene
84
85	The sidebar is working memory, not storage. Aim for three to seven hot spaces
86	per machine; everything else lives in `dev ls`.
87
88	`dev sweep` reports live sessions with no task recorded, which is usually where
89	the excess is. For each one, either `dev start` in that directory to track it,
90	or just close it — now that closing is not the same as forgetting.
91
92	## Agents are processes, not bookmarks
93
94	An agent pane with useful context in it is tempting to leave running forever.
95	Don't: herdr surfaces a resumable `agent_session` id, and `dev` stores it on
96	the task, so the conversation can be resumed after the process is gone.
97
98	Structure the isolation this way:
99
100	```
101	one independent change stream
102	        → one worktree
103	        → one workspace
104	        → N tabs / panes
105	        → N agents
106	```
107
108	Not one worktree per agent.
109
110	## Without herdr
111
112	`dev` selects `herdr` → `tmux` → `none`, in that order, and `runtime.backend`
113	pins it explicitly. The `none` backend prints a `cd` directive for the shell
114	wrapper instead of opening a session — so every core operation still works with
115	nothing but git installed.
116
